title: Waiting Well for the King
overview: Jesus gives three pictures of the time before his return and the judgment that follows, about being ready, using what you are given, and caring for people in need.

parts.label: Waiting for the groom (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: At weddings then, the groom came, often at night, to bring his bride to the feast, and young women met him with lamps to light the way. Five brought spare oil in case the wait was long, and five did not.

parts.label: The door is shut (vv. 6-13)
parts.note: This follows Jesus' words about his return in the chapter before, and verse 13 gives the point: be ready even if the wait is long, because readiness cannot be borrowed at the last minute. The story never says what the oil stands for, and readers have suggested faith, good deeds or God's Spirit.

parts.label: Money put in trust (vv. 14-23)
parts.note: A talent, which the NIV calls a 'bag of gold,' was a huge sum, worth many years of a laborer's wages. Most read the master as Jesus and the money as whatever God gives people to use while he is away, and those who use it well are given more and share their master's joy.

parts.label: The buried money (vv. 24-30)
parts.note: Afraid of a harsh master, the third servant hid the money and did nothing with it, so it is taken from him and he is thrown out into darkness and grief. Most read this as a warning against fearful inaction, though some modern readers see the master as a greedy landlord and side with the servant who would not play along.

parts.label: The king judges the nations (vv. 31-40)
parts.note: Jesus pictures the Son of Man, his usual name for himself, as a king judging all nations and sorting them the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats in a mixed flock. Those who fed, sheltered, clothed and visited people in need are invited into the kingdom, and they are surprised to hear they were caring for the king himself.

parts.label: Those sent away (vv. 41-46)
parts.note: Those who did nothing for people in need are sent to 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment,' and the text does not soften this. Most Christians through history have read it as punishment without end, while some read it as final destruction and a few hope for eventual restoration.

disagreement: Christians differ over who the king means in verse 40 by the least of his family, which the translations word slightly differently: many say any person in need, while others note that Jesus calls his followers his brothers elsewhere in Matthew and think he means how people treat his disciples.
think: How much do you think the small, unnoticed kindnesses in a life reveal about who a person really is?
